opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the one that stands out most to me is interaction length. Right now you can have a consistent, interactive experience for a few minutes, and that's a big step up from where we were with earlier versions. But if you want an agent to learn really long-horizon behaviors, or you want a world you can come back to and find things exactly where you left them, a few minutes isn't enough. Memory and consistency over much longer timescales is something we're actively thinking about.

Close behind that is the action space. What you can do directly as the agent is still fairly limited: moving around, navigating. We have promptable world events, where you can use text to change the world and make something happen, but that isn't the same as rich, fine-grained agency inside the environment. For the embodied agent research we care about, you'd really want the agent to manipulate objects and interact with other agents in complex ways. Modeling multiple independent agents acting in the same world, in a way that stays coherent, is still pretty hard.

There are smaller things too. Text rendering isn't always clean unless you specify it in the prompt, and the model won't perfectly reproduce real-world locations with geographic accuracy. But if I had to pick one, it's the horizon. Going from minutes to something much longer, while keeping the world consistent, would unlock a lot, both for training agents and for the kinds of experiences people could have in these worlds.

r001.rationale: The response says complex interaction with other agents is limited and that modeling multiple independent agents in the same world coherently remains difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
The one I keep coming back to is the interaction horizon. Genie 3 is a real step up from Genie 2 in that you can stay in a world for a few minutes rather than ten or twenty seconds, and it holds visual memory over that span, which was the thing I honestly didn't expect to work as well as it did. But a few minutes is still a few minutes. If you want an agent to learn something genuinely long-horizon, like exploring a building, coming back later, and finding things where it left them, we're not there yet. The world stays coherent far longer than before, but eventually consistency degrades, and you can't really run the kind of extended episodes that a proper RL curriculum would want.

Closely tied to that is the action space. We've moved to being able to steer the world with text-based promptable events, which is powerful, but the agent's own actions are still fairly constrained. You can navigate, you can do a limited set of interactions, but you can't yet express the full richness of what you'd want an embodied agent to be able to do, and the model doesn't always simulate complex multi-agent dynamics accurately either. Text rendering is also still unreliable unless it's in the prompt. So I'd frame it as: the fidelity and the real-time generation are impressive, but the horizon and the breadth of interaction are where the real research questions still sit, and those are exactly the things that matter if you believe, as I do, that world models are a route toward training more general agents.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Genie 3 does not always simulate complex multi-agent dynamics accurately, which describes an accuracy limitation. It does not identify the absence of multi-agent interactions in the simulated worlds.

astra-6.text: For me, it’s long-term consistency. Generating a convincing moment is one thing; keeping a world coherent as you interact with it is a much harder problem. If you change something, leave, and come back, you want that change to persist. That’s the limitation I’d focus on, because it really matters if you want to use these worlds for learning and planning.

r001.rationale: The response identifies long-term consistency and persistence as limitations, but does not mention the absence of multi-agent interactions.
